summary: STIR attests the identity of a caller using signed tokens, to fight robocall spoofing. This document explores applying STIR's PASSporT tokens and certificate framework to text and multimedia messaging, where similar impersonation occurs. It covers messages carried in SIP requests as well as other messaging systems.

eli5.summary: Phone calls can have a signature that proves who is really calling. This explains how to give text messages the same signature, so fakers are easier to spot.

questions: how does stir work for text messages
subtitle: How STIR's signed caller-identity tokens can be extended to protect text and multimedia messages from spoofed senders.

tldr.problem: STIR signs telephone calls to stop caller-number impersonation, but spammers and fraudsters also impersonate senders of text and multimedia messages.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a new PASSporT type, "msg", and an optional "msgi" claim that carries a digest of the message body, and it reuses existing STIR certificates.
tldr.outcome: SIP-based messaging can be protected against spoofing and nuisance messages, but the RFC notes that most messaging today runs over other protocols that this does not cover.

today: RFC 9475 is a Proposed Standard, published in December 2023, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. The RFC itself notes that its protection covers SIP-based messaging only.

sections.title: Why Messages Need STIR Too
sections.content:
The STIR work started with telephone calls. RFC 8224 defines a SIP Identity header that can carry a PASSporT (RFC 8225), a signed token that attests the caller is authorized to use the calling number.

The RFC points out that bulk, unsolicited commercial communication is not limited to calls. Spammers and fraudsters increasingly use messaging applications. Analysing message content is one defence, but as encrypted messaging becomes more common, content analysis may stop being reliable. The RFC also mentions emergency services, where messaging is increasingly used and identity assurance could help against denial-of-service and swatting attacks.

So the document explores applying PASSporT to textual and multimedia messaging, focusing on messages whose sender identity is a telephone number, and reusing existing STIR certificates. It mixes normative text (new claims) with informative guidance.
sections.eli5: Scammers fake who they are in text messages just like in phone calls. The same kind of signed name tag used for calls can be used for messages.

sections.title: Two Ways to Protect Messages
sections.content:
A PASSporT signature over the calling and called numbers plus a timestamp could already help against impersonation in number-based messaging. The RFC describes two broad ways PASSporT can apply:

  • A PASSporT secures the negotiation of a session over which messages are then exchanged.
  • In sessionless cases, a PASSporT is generated per message with its own built-in message security.

The first case needs little new work. The second needs an extension to the PASSporT claims.
sections.eli5: You can check someone's name tag once when a chat starts, or you can put a name tag on every single note they pass you.

sections.title: Message Sessions
sections.content:
In the first case, SIP negotiates a session whose media is text messages or MIME content, for example with the Message Session Relay Protocol (MSRP, RFC 4975). An INVITE with an Identity header carrying a PASSporT with the proper calling and called numbers would negotiate an MSRP session the same way an INVITE negotiates an audio session for a call. The RFC says this could apply to MSRP sessions negotiated for Rich Communication Suite (RCS).

If TLS secures MSRP, fingerprints of the TLS keys could be secured with the mky claim of PASSporT, using the framework in RFC 8862. Real-time text over RTP that can run over DTLS/SRTP should work with mky too. For the most basic cases, STIR for messaging should need no further protocol enhancements.

There are limits. Current use of the Identity header is largely confined to INVITE requests that start calls, and RCS-style applications would need PASSporTs for all participants, which could get complex in multiparty conversations. That would likely need STIR connected identity, and PASSporT-signed session conferencing is out of scope. The assurance is also only between an authentication service and a verification service, so tampering is still possible before signing and after verification. STIR aims at spoofed origination more than machine-in-the-middle attacks.
sections.eli5: If two people start a chat room, the doorman checks the name tags once at the door. After that, everyone inside is trusted as much as the doorman is.

sections.title: The msg Type and msgi Claim
sections.content:
The second case uses the SIP MESSAGE method (RFC 3428), which carries a message in the request body. An Identity header could be added to any MESSAGE, but without a new claim the PASSporT would not protect the content, and could be reused in cut-and-paste attacks, where the header from a legitimate request is attached to a request for a different user. S/MIME (RFC 8591) is one alternative for integrity, and PASSporT can also provide its own check.

To tell message PASSporTs apart from call PASSporTs, the RFC defines a new msg PASSporT type. A msg PASSporT may carry a new optional JWT claim, msgi, which is a digest over the MIME body holding the text or multimedia message. Authentication services MUST NOT include msgi in other PASSporT types, and verification services MUST ignore it there. It is OPTIONAL in msg PASSporTs because integrity may come from some other service.

The value of msgi is the hash algorithm name, a hyphen, and the base64-encoded digest of the canonicalized MIME body. Implementations MUST support SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512, identified as sha256, sha384 and sha512. They MAY support additional recommended algorithms from the IANA COSE Algorithms registry. Algorithm identifiers MUST be lowercase and MUST NOT contain hyphens.

If a SIP verification service wants to tell the sender that the msgi hash does not match the received message, a SIP 438 response code is the most appropriate.
sections.eli5: The sender puts the message in a sealed envelope and writes a fingerprint of it on the name tag. If someone swaps the letter, the fingerprint will not match.

sections.title: Delivery, Replay and Multiparty Messages
sections.content:
Messages may be stored and forwarded, so delivery can happen minutes or hours after sending. The expiry freshness window recommended by RFC 8224 may then be too strict, and relaxing it needs support on the receiving side. Replay risk is largely reduced by the PASSporT timestamp: duplicates are easy to detect, and the timestamp can order the inbox so stale messages are not shown as fresh.

For a MESSAGE sent over SIP, the PASSporT travels in an Identity header and follows the RFC 8224 procedures plus the msgi claim. Other protocols might carry PASSporTs themselves, and where legacy systems cannot (the RFC names Short Message Peer-to-Peer systems that cannot be upgraded), out-of-band conveyance (RFC 8816) would be the only way. Interaction with email-style tools used for MMS, such as DMARC, is out of scope.

A MESSAGE can go to several destinations, and the dest claim can list multiple targets without one PASSporT per target. If an intermediary forks the request and the authentication service did not know the target list, the intermediary would need diversion PASSporTs (RFC 8946). In some CPIM environments, intermediaries may modify CPIM headers, which would break MIME-layer integrity, so such environments need a profile limited to the CPIM payload.
sections.eli5: A letter might sit in the mailbox for hours before it is read. The date stamp on it tells you whether it is old news, and it stops someone from handing you the same letter twice.

sections.title: Certificates
sections.content:
STIR certificates (RFC 8226) attest a Service Provider Code and/or a set of telephone numbers through the TNAuthList. The RFC proposes that these semantics suffice for signing messages from a telephone number without modification.

The certificate named by the PASSporT x5u can change over time through expiry or rollover, and short-lived certificates may roll over daily or more often. A store-and-forward messaging system must allow for a certificate that was valid when the PASSporT was made but expires before the user reads the message. That might require storing an indicator of validity at receipt time, or storing the certificate with the PASSporT so the iat claim can be compared with the certificate's freshness window.

Because orig and dest may hold URIs without telephone numbers, the mechanism is not inherently restricted to telephone numbers, though the RFC gives no guidance on certification authorities for such values.
sections.eli5: The name tag is vouched for by an official stamp. Stamps can expire, so a mailbox must remember whether the stamp was good when the letter arrived.

sections.title: Privacy, Security and IANA
sections.content:
The RFC inherits the security considerations of RFC 8224, plus those of SIP messaging in RFC 3428 and RFC 8591. Implementers should also heed the store-and-forward and replay guidance above.

On privacy, signing has little direct effect. An authentication service computing msgi over a cleartext message will see its contents, which it might not otherwise. A msg PASSporT adds no privacy protection to the content.

The RFC also notes that most messaging to and from telephone numbers today uses protocols other than SIP, so this capability only mitigates spoofing and nuisance messaging for SIP-based platforms. IANA added the msgi claim (Message Integrity Information) to the JSON Web Token Claims registry and the msg type to the PASSporT Extensions registry.
sections.eli5: The name tag shows who sent a note, but it does not hide the note. It also only works in the mail system that uses name tags.

items.title: Message sessions
items.text: A PASSporT in an INVITE negotiates a session such as MSRP, with little change to RFC 8224.

items.title: Individual messages
items.text: A msg PASSporT with a msgi digest protects each SIP MESSAGE body.
